title: Amazon MGM Studios Japan ‘Doubling’ Investment to Meet Global Standards, Local Chief Buddy Marini Reveals at Tokyo Market
description: Amazon MGM Studios Japan is doubling its investment to bring its content up to global standards, studio head Buddy Marini said Wednesday at a Tokyo
body:
Amazon MGM Studios Japan is doubling its investment to bring its content up to global standards, studio head Buddy Marini said Wednesday at a Tokyo International Film Festival TIFFCOM market session on unlocking the global potential of Japanese IP.

	The session, organized by the Motion Picture Association (MPA) and UniJapan, also featured Credeus CEO Matsuhashi Shinzo and “One Piece” Netflix series executive producer Steven Maeda, with entertainment sociologist and consultant Nakayama Atsuo serving as moderator.
	

	Marini, who was appointed head of the Japan studio in March, is in charge of its homegrown film, series and anime productions. He previously served as managing director of Warner Bros. Discovery Japan and CEO of Hulu Japan, and founded Mangamo.

	He began by explaining how his platform “manages everything – from the initial idea stage through planning, development, strategy, investment, and all the way to the final product.”

	The basic strategy for both Japan and the Amazon studio as a whole, he added, is to “expand into the global market.” “There are all kinds of viewers, so the goal is to reach all of them,” he said. “So we’re handling all kinds of content, regardless of genre.”

	That is also true of other platforms, but Marini believes that Amazon is unique in offering various benefits to its Prime members – movies being among them. “Our primary objective has always been to delight the audience in that specific country or region,” he said. “But in doing that we’ve started to make our mark in various places around the world. Since our service is global, our audience isn’t really concerned with which country the content is from. They just think, ‘If it’s interesting, it’s interesting.’ So, we’re doubling our investment to ensure that quality meets global standards.”
	

	Among upcoming projects on his studio’s slate are “The Apothecary Diaries,” a live-action adaptation of a bestselling historical mystery franchise, and “Bless,” a live-action adaptation of a hit manga about an aspiring makeup artist.

	Among past Japanese-language hits on Amazon Prime is “The Silent Service,” a live-action series about a rogue Japanese submarine captain who hijacks a U.S. sub, based on a long-running manga that also generated a hit anime series. “We’ve achieved some amazing results with the series,” commented Marini, “but it’s difficult to maintain that level of quality.”

	“When it comes to elevating our content to IPs that can resonate globally, I truly believe that the reverse-engineering process is the most important factor,” Marini said. “So, within our team, the creative staff works closely with the screenwriters to develop the scripts and ensure that from a global perspective, we’re crafting a story that’s truly compelling.”

	Also on the panel was Matsuhashi, whose credits as producer include last year’s smash “Kokuho,” which set an all-time box office record for Japanese live-action films, as well as the “Kingdom” period action series, the “Gintama” action comedy series, “Blue Lock” and “Golden Kamuy.” He joined Wowow in 1994, made his producing debut with “Battle Royale,” went independent in 2005 and started his present company, Credeus, about eight years ago. “I realized I wouldn’t be able to make the kind of work I envisioned unless I did that, so that’s the choice I made,” he said.

	As a producer Matsuhashi has developed what he calls the “right production ratio.” “First and foremost, the story has to be interesting,” he said. “Then it needs to be turned into an interesting script. Then you bring in an excellent director and crew and assemble a great cast. I believe that only when these elements come together does a work come as close as possible to success.”

	The proof that this “ratio” is indeed right is Matsuhashi’s sterling track record – the films he has produced passed JPY100 billion ($633 million) in cumulative box office this year.

	His breakthrough was the “Kingdom” historical action/drama series, which is set in China’s Warring States period and is based on a popular manga. Launched in 2019, it now totals five feature entries.
	

	The start, Matsuhashi said, came when Sanford Panitch, who was then in charge of international production for Sony Pictures, approached him about making local films for Japan. “I asked him if he wanted to fill a production quota with three films or revolutionize Japanese movies,” Matsuhashi recalled. When Panitch opted for the latter, Matsuhashi brought him a concept for three “Kingdom” films. “I told him that the three-film package was a single business venture, so I wanted him to invest in it. I doubt there are many projects created with this kind of specific plan in mind.”

	Panitch signed on and the first three films each earned more than JPY5 billion ($31.7 million) – making them major hits at the Japanese box office. The moral: A bold vision, made with the right elements, can yield big returns.

	Starting more than two decades ago, Matsuhashi has also negotiated a success fee for all of his projects. “It was something that hadn’t really been mainstream in Japan,” he said. “I’ve continued using this model for a long time – where the producer, the person actually creating the work, receives a success fee if it becomes a hit – and it’s gradually become established.”

	Rounding out the panel was Maeda, executive producer of the Netflix live-action series “One Piece,” which topped the charts in 46 countries in its opening week in 2023 and racked up more than 140 million viewing hours over those first seven days. He also worked on “Lost,” “The X-Files” and “Lie to Me,” and is now adapting “Monstress,” the Eisner-winning graphic novel, for Amazon Prime Video alongside his partner Tiff Greshler and Hivemind Entertainment.

	When he was approached by Tomorrow Studios about making a live-action version of “One Piece,” Maeda said he knew nothing about the manga, but “read the first hundred chapters… and I just loved it.” But he also wondered how they could make the series “since it was going to be so expensive.”

	When Netflix became involved, Maeda remembered, “they wanted us to make it as cheaply as possible.” But he knew that fans would not be happy with a cut-rate “One Piece.” “They didn’t want us to make a bad version of one of their favorite anime or manga,” he said, “so we had to go in there and really convince (Netflix) that by making a show fans would appreciate, they also would attract a new audience.”
	

	“That’s the battle of a lot of global IP,” he added. “You’re going to have people who love the show, and they want a faithful adaptation of that show. You’re going to have people who have never heard of the show, and you still need to bring those people in as well.”

	“And if you succeed, you can have an international success,” Maeda said. “And if you fail, everyone hates you.”

schema.headline: Amazon MGM Studios Japan ‘Doubling’ Investment to Meet Global Standards, Local Chief Buddy Marini Reveals at Tokyo Market

title: Thai Forest Spirit Horror ‘Cher,’ First Thai Winner at Frontières, Joins Tokyo Gap-Financing Market
description: A Thai horror film built on the folklore of the Nang Mai, the forest nymphs of Thai myth, is the only Thai entry in the 2026 Tokyo Gap-Financing Ma
body:
A Thai horror film built on the folklore of the Nang Mai, the forest nymphs of Thai myth, is the only Thai entry in the 2026 Tokyo Gap-Financing Market lineup. 

	“Cher” arrives in Tokyo after becoming the first Thai project selected for, and awarded a top prize at, Canada’s Frontières Co-Production Market.

	Benetone Films and Fearfolks are producing the feature, which Songsak Mongkolthong (“Graveyard Horror,” “School Tales the Series”) directs from a screenplay by Patrick Graham, writer of Netflix’s “Ghoul” and “Betaal.”
	

	Rattanawadee “Mim” Wongthong (“Death Whisperer”) heads the cast, with Pae Arak and Weir Sukollawat (“4 Tigers”). Vikash Nowlakha, who shot the “Dhurandhar” duology, is the cinematographer. The producers said those two Indian films earned a combined $330 million at the global box office.

	Mongkolthong said the story raises the possibility that the Nang Mai, long part of Thai belief, may have different origins from the ones taught in Thailand.

	“The idea of starting a new life begins with confronting our own prejudices, anger, and hatred. When we learn to move beyond anger and hatred, a new life can begin,” he said.

	Benetone Films CEO Rachvin Narula and COO Kulthep Narula said the company backed the project from the outset and treated it, as the studio’s first tentpole, differently from the approach of other Thai studios.

	“We are absolutely thrilled it is getting the global recognition it deserves so early on,” they said.

	Tokyo is the latest stop on a market run for the film. It was selected for the It Project market at the Network of Asian Fantastic Films (NAFF), part of South Korea’s Bucheon International Fantastic Film Festival (BIFAN), and won at Frontières in July.
	

	“We are extremely grateful to BIFAN, Frontières and TIFFCOM for giving Thai films a voice on this global stage, and for allowing us to bear these great honors,” said Fearfolks CEO Hans Audric Estialbo. “Prestigious markets like TIFFCOM allow the film to build momentum and a community of followers early, which is what most successful IPs need now.”

	Filming is due to start in the first three months of 2027, ahead of a global release in 2028.

	The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival.

schema.headline: Thai Forest Spirit Horror ‘Cher,’ First Thai Winner at Frontières, Joins Tokyo Gap-Financing Market

title: Korean Webtoon Adaptations, ‘The Vanishing Act’ Lead 2027 Vertical Slate Unveiled by COL Group, V47 and Virtue Asia
description: Adaptations of Korean webtoons and web novels developed with CJ Group and a batch of new originals headline the 2027 vertical slate unveiled in Sin
body:
Adaptations of Korean webtoons and web novels developed with CJ Group and a batch of new originals headline the 2027 vertical slate unveiled in Singapore on Wednesday by FlareFlow parent COL Group, V47 Entertainment and Virtue Asia.

	The lineup was presented at Inside Microdramas, which organizers described as an upfront without precedent.

	The Korean titles, developed with CJ Group, include “Idol Once Again,” a fantasy in which a washed-up idol travels back in time for a second shot at fame, and “Genius Doctor Lee Mu-jin,” based on a popular webtoon about a street fighter coached by the ghost of a brilliant physician. Also on the Korean slate is “The Exclusive Secretary,” adapted from a web novel, in which a corporate heir and the secretary who lives with him grow closer while a perilous fight over the family succession plays out.
	

	On the originals side, COL Group and V47 are developing “The Vanishing Act,” a mystery about a magician who disappears on air during the final of an international talent contest, and “Fortune Chasers,” which mixes a scripted reality competition with thriller beats. “1% Better,” a reality format set in the world of sports and fitness, pits unlikely rivals against each other.

	The slate also carries over three of COL’s best-performing existing microdramas – “Oops, I Married My Bestie’s Brother!,” “My Sweetheart’s a Gangster” and “From Janitor to Mrs. Billionaire” – as IP the companies aim to extend through wider distribution, adaptation and commercial tie-ups. They did not specify what form those follow-ups will take.
	

	COL Group’s FlareFlow has passed 52 million registered users and carries close to 7,000 short-drama titles, reaching viewers in upward of 200 countries and regions. The platform topped all rights holders in TikTok’s short-drama revenue-share rankings for the first quarter of 2026.

	The three companies also launched Story Engine, an operating model that ties together development, production, financing and worldwide distribution. It pools V47’s development and production arm, Virtue Asia’s expertise in cultural strategy and integrating brands, and COL Group’s genre know-how and international distribution reach. Brands can go past product placement and sponsorship to come aboard as development partners, executive producers or financiers, with a possible stake in the resulting IP.

	“We see a real opportunity for brands to go beyond traditional advertising and become part of the entertainment audiences actively choose to watch,” said Timothy Oh, chief marketing officer of FlareFlow and general manager of COL Group International. “By bringing together our genre expertise and international distribution network with the creative strengths of V47 and Virtue, we’re helping brands develop original entertainment IP that can build lasting audience connections and grow across platforms and markets.”

	V47 was formed by Virtue Asia and Goldfinch International, the U.K.-based Goldfinch Group’s international expansion vehicle, which targets MENA, Asia and Africa. 

	V47 Entertainment chair David Webster said the opportunity lay in developing entertainment that could grow into something larger than one production. “By bringing brands into the development and financing process, we can give ambitious original ideas the backing they need to reach audiences, while creating opportunities to build franchises and valuable IP over time. The story must always come first, but we’re opening up new ways for brands to become meaningful partners in creating the entertainment people want to watch.”

	Virtue Asia, a strategic and creative agency, counts Disney, Google, Spotify, Toyota, Diageo and Shiseido among its clients. Its CEO, Lesley John, said brands could no longer get noticed by interrupting culture and instead had to earn a place within it. “Microdramas offer an exciting opportunity, but success depends on understanding the culture, the audience, and the storytelling that makes people want to keep watching. Our role is to bring those worlds together – translating cultural insight into creative integration that feels native to the story and adds value to the audience experience, not just visibility for the brand.”

schema.headline: Korean Webtoon Adaptations, ‘The Vanishing Act’ Lead 2027 Vertical Slate Unveiled by COL Group, V47 and Virtue Asia

title: Kore-eda Hirokazu Hails Japanese Cinema’s Global Moment as Ninomiya Kazunari, Academy’s Amy Homma and ‘Kokuho’ Producer Murata Chieko Take Stage at Kering Women in Motion Tokyo Event
description: Kering Women in Motion, an allied program of the Tokyo International Film Festival, held a talk event on Tuesday at Toho Cinemas Roppongi Hills for
body:
Kering Women in Motion, an allied program of the Tokyo International Film Festival, held a talk event on Tuesday at Toho Cinemas Roppongi Hills for a packed crowd.

	Director Kore-eda Hirokazu (“Shoplifters”) opened the event with brief remarks. “In recent years, I’ve been hearing people at international film festivals say, ‘Japanese films are really interesting right now.’ That’s a sentiment we didn’t hear 10 years ago,” he said. “Led by Hamaguchi Ryusuke and Fukada Koji, directors in their 20s and 30s have been taking their works overseas, and through their accumulated efforts and recognition, the attention given to Japanese films has been increasing. How to pass this on to the next generation and spread it further is a challenge for the older generation, and I think it’s also very important for film fans who are exposed to these works.”
	

	The panelists – Arashi singer and actor Ninomiya Kazunari, producer Murata Chieko and Amy Homma, director and president of the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and Academy Collection – spoke about the present and future of Japanese cinema, as well as diversity and inclusion in the industry, with journalist Tatsuta Atsuko serving as facilitator.

	“I’m a Japanese-American woman and I’m a Jewish American woman – and both of those cultures and ethnicities carry deeply long lineages of history,” Homma said. “I’m very lucky to have been raised with the awareness that multiple truths can exist at the same time.”

	National cinemas also exist parallel to each other, she added, but “that does not make one more important or one more harder than the other,” she said. “American film history is just as important as Japanese film history and just as important as French film history.”
	

	By taking a broad view of film history and experiencing different types of cinema, she said, “We allow ourselves to learn so much more about a lived experience that’s outside of our own, because there’s no better way to develop empathy to develop cultural understanding than through watching a movie.”

	Ninomiya, who first came to international attention for his starring role in Clint Eastwood’s Academy Award-winning World War II drama “Letters from Iwo Jima,” said that working on an international production “presented both differences and learning opportunities for me as an actor.” One difference, he found, was the staff’s tendency “to ask more questions” than they would on a Japanese set. “They ask things like, ‘What is this?’ or ‘How do you use this?’” The result, he said, was a conversation leading to solutions, instead of a top-down explanation that might result in confusion.

	Murata, the producer of the 2025 smash-hit kabuki-themed drama “Kokuho,” which received rave reviews abroad and was nominated for a Best Makeup and Hairstyling Oscar, said she wanted to “create something that will move as many people as possible, make as many people laugh as possible, and make as many people cry as possible.”

	For that to happen, she added, tolerance of varying cultural perspectives is essential. “The worst case is a world in which that becomes difficult,” she said.

	Homma commented that as a museum director in charge of various teams doing everything from research to marketing, “It’s always about who the best person would be.” Her aim, she added, was “for many people to bring their own cultural differences or their own unique qualities and have that be seen as a strength. I don’t want anyone to shy or hide their individualism.”

	Diversity “across gender expression, across ethnicity and across ages,” she said, “is what makes for a great team,” adding, “It’s about plural thinking, not individual thinking.”

schema.headline: Kore-eda Hirokazu Hails Japanese Cinema’s Global Moment as Ninomiya Kazunari, Academy’s Amy Homma and ‘Kokuho’ Producer Murata Chieko Take Stage at Kering Women in Motion Tokyo Event

title: Camila Mendes, Leslie Bibb Shooting ‘Upgraded 2’ in Venice, Where Biennale Art Show Is Part of Rom-Com’s Storyline
description: Shooting is underway in Venice on “Upgraded 2,” the sequel to Amazon MGM Studios’ buzzy 2024 rom-com “Upgraded” that, as announced, is set to star
body:
Shooting is underway in Venice on “Upgraded 2,” the sequel to Amazon MGM Studios’ buzzy 2024 rom-com “Upgraded” that, as announced, is set to star Leslie Bibb alongside Camila Mendes.

	Mendes is returning to the franchise as Ana Santos, an intern at a New York City auction house who feigns a higher job status after she is upgraded to first class on her flight to London. During the flight, she impresses a wealthy young Englishman named William who is connected to the high-society art world, played by Archie Renaux.
	

	In the sequel to the modern-day “Cinderella” tale, on which cameras started rolling in Venice on Oct. 21, Ana is now seemingly seeking to make her mark at the Venice Biennale art exhibition, the world’s oldest contemporary art fair. Becca Gleason, who is helming the sequel — taking over from “Upgraded” director Carlson Young — has been shooting on the terrace of Ca’ Giustinian, the Biennale headquarters that overlook the lagoon’s Grand Canal; in the neo-Gothic Palazzo Franchetti near the Accademia bridge, which serves as a Biennale exhibition space; and at the luxurious Moro Venice restaurant. So far, there are no indications on what Bibb’s role is.

	Luke Roberts and Justin Matthews, who penned the first film, also wrote the screenplay for the sequel.

	Besides Venice and the Biennale, “Upgraded 2″ will have a decidedly Italian flavor. Following 12 days of shooting on the lagoon, principal photography will move to Rome where 33 more days of shooting are planned, according to Italy for Movies, the country’s national portal for film and TV production locations and incentives. The production designer is Italy’s Luca Tranchino (“Prison Break,” “Domina”). The Italian company serving as executive producer on the sequel is Colorado Film.
	

	Producers on “Upgraded 2″ include Mike Karz and Bill Bindley for Gulfstream Pictures, Mendes and Rachel Matthews for Honor Role, Lena Roklin for Luber Roklin Entertainment and Piers Tempest for Tempo Production.



	

									andrea avezzu

title: Val Chmerkovskiy Says He Wants ‘Nothing But Love’ for Carrie Ann Inaba Following ‘DWTS’ Suspension, Apologizes to Jenna Dewan: ‘I Am So Sorry for All the Chaos’
description: “Dancing With the Stars” pro Val Chmerkovskiy and judge Carrie Ann Inaba have made amends, concluding the hectic saga that has ensued since Chmerko
body:
“Dancing With the Stars” pro Val Chmerkovskiy and judge Carrie Ann Inaba have made amends, concluding the hectic saga that has ensued since Chmerkovskiy made an “inappropriate” joke about Inaba earlier this month that resulted in his getting benched from the competition.

	On Tuesday night’s episode of the dance competition series, Chmerkovskiy was back in the ballroom following a one-week suspension from the show. The decision by the show to remove him from the competition temporarily was made after Chmerkovskiy posted to his TikTok story, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night,” after his wife, fellow judge Jenna Johnson, was critiqued by Inaba during the Oct. 13 episode of the show. The TikTok was interpreted as a reference to Will Smith’s infamous slap at the 2022 Oscars, and deemed “inappropriate” by BBC Studios.
	

	While Chmerkovskiy’s absence was not touched upon in last week’s episode, this week, as Val returned, audiences saw the pro apologize to his partner, Jenna Dewan. “We are back together. I am so sorry for all the chaos. You did not sign up for that, and I feel awful,” Chmerkovskiy said during their pre-dance package, to which Dewan responded: “I forgive you…I missed you.”

	Following Tuesday’s show, Chmerkovskiy and Inaba embraced one another, as caught on camera across social media. “It felt [like] cathartic relief, you know?” Chmerkovskiy told People about speaking with Inaba. “I think it was just really important for me to make sure that she feels safe and knows that, firsthand from me, I want nothing but love for her.”
	

	He continued: “I want nothing but joy for her and as much as the world might say otherwise, I want her to know how I feel, not how others want me to feel, but how I genuinely feel. I will have nothing but love for Carrie Ann. I have nothing but respect for what she has to say.”

	Earlier on Tuesday, Inaba posted a lengthy statement to Instagram about the saga. “I have not spoken about what happened because of professional courtesy for those who are still competing, and we actually have standards and practices that keep us separated,” Inaba began. 

	“But I think a part of this ‘headline’ has missed a few important parts of what happened,” Inaba continued. “I think it’s important for everyone to know that Jenna and I hugged it out after the Super Bowl show. Jenna was an absolute professional about it, and two women worked through the moment. It came to my attention later that Jenna was deeply hurt. So I also offered to speak with her at any time. I have also offered to discuss the lift rule and how I enforce it. @sharnaburgess made a great video explaining lifts, assists and which dances allow and don’t allow them.”

	“I think in the future, a new lift rule should be created for next season,” she concluded. “Working together to create a better understanding between the dancers and the judges and our audience is important to me, as we move forward and is something I have asked for.”

schema.headline: Val Chmerkovskiy Says He Wants ‘Nothing But Love’ for Carrie Ann Inaba Following ‘DWTS’ Suspension, Apologizes to Jenna Dewan: ‘I Am So Sorry for All the Chaos’

title: Academy CEO Bill Kramer Maps Oscars’ Global Ambitions in Tokyo: ‘Parasite’ Win Was ‘a Pivot, a Shift’
description: The Academy plans to keep taking the Oscars global, from recruiting members in underrepresented countries to streaming the ceremony free on YouTube
body:
The Academy plans to keep taking the Oscars global, from recruiting members in underrepresented countries to streaming the ceremony free on YouTube, its leadership said in Tokyo, where CEO Bill Kramer said the share of members living outside the U.S. has grown from around 5% to 25% in a decade.

	Kramer was speaking at an Academy in Tokyo panel at the Tokyo International Film Festival alongside Academy president Lynette Howell Taylor and chief membership, impact and industry officer Meredith Shea, moderated by festival director Hisamatsu Takeo. The festival also presented Kramer with its Global Cinema Leadership Special Award.
	

	Kramer described the membership shift as part of a push for a more diverse and inclusive Academy. A decade ago, he said, only 5% to 6% of members were based outside the U.S. “Now it’s 25%, and that number is growing.” The Academy has about 70 members in Japan.

	“People are making movies around the world, people are watching films that are not in their native language more and more,” Kramer said. “We’re making movies everywhere, we’re viewing movies in a much more nimble and accessible way, and the Academy needs to reflect that.”

	Kramer pointed out that every category at the most recent Oscars had international representation, including best picture. “Of course, everybody remembers the moment when ‘Parasite’ won. It was sort of a pivot, a shift, I think, in our thinking about what was possible with global cinema at the Oscars, and that continues,” he said, referring to Bong Joon Ho’s 2020 best picture winner.
	

	Howell Taylor explained that besides Oscar nominees, who are automatically put forward, and candidates sponsored by existing members, each branch has an Aperture committee charged with finding filmmakers around the world. “And each year, we have very specific focus for countries that are potentially underrepresented,” she said.

	During the audience Q&A, Howell Taylor said: “Just because the membership has increased does not mean that the qualifications have somehow decreased. Our membership was smaller because we were not as global, and we weren’t looking for excellence in filmmakers as much outside of the U.S.”

	Over the past couple of years, the Academy has visited India, London, Rio, Morelia, Marrakech and Busan. “We’re thrilled to be here in Tokyo, and you’ll be seeing us do that more and more,” Kramer said, adding that the Academy’s city-by-city member events will continue “all over the world.” This was, he said, the Academy’s “first official Academy trip to the Tokyo Film Festival, but it won’t be our last.”

	Being Academy president, Howell Taylor said, “is an incredible privilege because I get to meet storytellers all around the world in this position.” She added: “I carry all the conversations that I have at various film festivals and member gatherings back to L.A. And it’s so crucial to take those conversations and that information because it really does shape the work that the Board does and how our organization moves forward.”

	Shea noted that submitting a film for Oscar consideration costs nothing in any category, more than 200 festival awards make short films automatically eligible, and members can watch contenders on the Academy Screening Room app. “That’s our deep commitment to global cinema, that we don’t want individuals to feel like it’s not open, that it is just an L.A.-based, Hollywood-centric organization. The Academy is global, and it welcomes all filmmakers,” she said.

	A major step toward a worldwide audience comes with the Oscars’ move to YouTube, where Kramer said the ceremony will be available free to 2.5 billion people in more than 30 languages from 2029. “So, for the first time, everyone around the world will have access to the show at the same time in the same format. And that is a huge, intentional move by the Academy to reach a bigger global audience,” he said.
	

	Asked whether the Tokyo International Film Festival could join the six festivals whose top prizes now qualify films for the international feature race, Kramer said: “We’re looking to expand the number of festivals that help films qualify for the International Feature Film category. That’s a process that we’re undertaking this year, so stay tuned for more information on that.”

	In a later answer, Kramer said the first six were chosen in large part on “the timing on the calendar,” and that the Academy is “just beginning these conversations.” Howell Taylor said discussions about expanding the list are “ongoing right now.”

	Asked whether the category could one day become redundant as the Academy grows more international, Kramer said: “Right now, I don’t see that category as being redundant.”

	Animation is another area where the Academy’s global reach shows. Shea, who ran the animated feature category for more than a decade, said submissions grew from 12 to close to 40 over that period, with at least six anime titles a year. “Japan has such a deep history of animated filmmaking,” said Kramer, who added that the Academy’s globalization “is good for all filmmakers, including Japanese filmmakers.”

	Speaking separately with Variety in Tokyo, Kramer, Howell Taylor, Shea and Academy Museum director and president Amy Homma also discussed AI, the festival route into the international feature race and the 2029 YouTube ceremony.

	In his closing remarks, Kramer said: “I’m always struck on these trips, and this is no exception, by the warmth, by the sense of community, by the sense of collaboration, and how we all speak the same cinema language. And it’s very heartening, especially in this moment of a lot of global complications and complexities.”

schema.headline: Academy CEO Bill Kramer Maps Oscars’ Global Ambitions in Tokyo: ‘Parasite’ Win Was ‘a Pivot, a Shift’

title: Japanese-Brazilian Grief Drama ‘Yellow Chrysanthemum,’ Set During the 2014 Soccer World Cup, Joins Tokyo Gap-Financing Market
description: A Japanese-Brazilian teenager forced to face a family loss nobody will talk about is at the heart of “Yellow Chrysanthemum,” the first feature from
body:
A Japanese-Brazilian teenager forced to face a family loss nobody will talk about is at the heart of “Yellow Chrysanthemum,” the first feature from Japanese-Brazilian director André Hayato Saito, which is among the projects at this year’s Tokyo Gap-Financing Market.

	The film is set in São Paulo in July 2014, while Brazil is staging the World Cup. Erika, 16, is a third-generation Japanese-Brazilian who feels like an outsider in the country she was born in and wants nothing to do with her family’s roots.
	

	That rejection stems from an old wound. When Erika was 7, her cousin Yam, who was also her closest friend, vanished during a traditional festival in the Liberdade neighborhood while Erika’s mother was looking after the children. The family has been locked in guilty silence ever since.

	Erika’s friendship with Bianca, a Black classmate mourning the recent death of her mother, stirs up the feelings she has long pushed down. Bianca makes no secret of her grief, and as the two girls grow closer, Erika’s family can no longer avoid confronting Yam’s absence.

	“I vividly remember being a little boy, sitting in the bathroom with my father, when I suddenly asked him where we go after we die. He paused for a moment and answered with a long and profound silence,” Saito said.

	Growing up in a Japanese-Brazilian household, Saito came to see how silence in his family could express love and respect while also hiding pain. His short films have dealt with grief, memory, identity and life between two cultures, and he described the feature as a continuation of that work.
	

	One of those shorts, “Amarela,” also follows a Japanese-Brazilian teenager named Erika who turns her back on her family’s traditions, this time over the course of a World Cup final between Brazil and France. It competed for the short film Palme d’Or at Cannes in 2024, was shortlisted for the live-action short Oscar at the 98th Academy Awards and won best live-action short at Brazil’s Grande Otelo Awards. It is part of a trilogy of shorts, with “Kokoro to Kokoro” and “Vento Dourado,” that Saito made with São Paulo-based MyMama Entertainment.

	“I don’t want to offer easy answers or a conventional sense of closure. I hope audiences will recognize something of their own families in Erika’s journey, regardless of their cultural backgrounds, and reflect on the things that remain unspoken in their own lives,” Saito said.

	The project, a co-production between Brazil, Japan, Germany and France, is now in pre-production after several years of development. It took part in TorinoFilmLab, where it won the TorinoFilmLab Production Award, and was also selected for Focus Copro at Cannes. The team plans to film a key sequence during a traditional Japanese Toro Nagashi ceremony in Brazil in November this year.

	Producer Mayra Faour Auad is the founder of MyMama Entertainment and produced “Amarela.” She has more than 20 credits, most of them international co-productions. MyMama is developing “Yellow Chrysanthemum” with One Two Films, Loaded Films and Blue Monday.

	In Tokyo, Faour Auad said the team wants to close the film’s financing gap and connect with producers, distributors and sales agents who could carry the film to audiences around Asia.

	“Given the film’s Japanese-Brazilian roots, finding an audience in Japan has particular meaning for us,” Faour Auad said.

	Saito is also developing his second feature, “Little Faults,” which earned a spot in Turin’s Boost IT Lab this year. Its protagonist is an aging Japanese-Brazilian woman living in Japan who starts committing minor offenses, hoping to land in prison, where she thinks she might at last be cared for and feel she belongs.

	The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival.

schema.headline: Japanese-Brazilian Grief Drama ‘Yellow Chrysanthemum,’ Set During the 2014 Soccer World Cup, Joins Tokyo Gap-Financing Market

title: Jessica Biel Says She Won’t Hand Her Son Acting Roles Just ‘Because You’re Part of This Family’: ‘We’re Not Doing That’
description: With parents like Jessica Biel and Justin Timberlake, it might not be entirely possible to avoid being labeled a nepo baby in totality — but that i
body:
With parents like Jessica Biel and Justin Timberlake, it might not be entirely possible to avoid being labeled a nepo baby in totality — but that isn’t stopping Biel from making it explicitly clear to her son that he “can’t just take a part” from someone because of who his parents are.

	On a recent episode of the “Great Chat Show” podcast, Biel told host Josh Smith that she’s been discussing the business of acting with her oldest son, 11-year-old Silas, who recently made an appearance in “Matchbox: The Movie,” in which Biel starred.
	

	“He’s a DJ, he’s incredible [at] music, he’s doing such cool things with music — he just has that, right? He just has that innately and is interested in that,” she said. “And also has this comedy streak and this theatrical kind of funny, silly quality. And he’s been talking to us about, yeah, wanting to be an actor. So, this is coming up a lot.”

	She explained that when Silas’ name came up for the role in “Matchbox,” she was initially unsure of moving forward, given that she and Timberlake try to keep their kids “away from all of this.” But, she said, “you don’t want to squash their dreams, even though I kind of want to squash this one. I’m like, ‘Please don’t do this! Anything but this! It’s really hard!’”

	Biel continued: “Because the other thing I was talking to him, Silas, about is, there are kids who work really hard, and they go to acting class, and they’re in theater class, and they’re doing all the work,” Biel explained. “You can’t just take a part from that person just because you’re my son. Like, that’s not cool. We’re not doing that. So this is a special opportunity because it’s really teeny tiny. And, if you had a big monologue, I wouldn’t let him do it… You would have to earn that part because we’re not starting that. We’re not starting, ‘Oh, you just get handed a bunch of opportunities because you’re part of this family.’ Mm-mm, we’re not doing that.”
	

	Biel first broke into Hollywood as Mary Camden on the long-running family drama “7th Heaven.” She’s currently a producer on a reboot of the show, which she said will “modernize it” and focus on “the things that are happening for teenagers and families that have teenagers all the way down to the youngest child — technology-based issues, school stuff, bullying stuff, drugs, alcohol.”

	She is also set to star in the forthcoming Searchlight film “Playmates” as Hugh Hefner’s wife.

schema.headline: Jessica Biel Says She Won’t Hand Her Son Acting Roles Just ‘Because You’re Part of This Family’: ‘We’re Not Doing That’

title: Taiwan-Japan Film Fund Daily Capital Launches at Tokyo Market, Backs Period Romance ‘Love Ends in Bloom’
description: Daily Capital, a new fund focused on Taiwan-Japan film and television co-productions, launched on the Tokyo International Film Festival market TIFF
body:
Daily Capital, a new fund focused on Taiwan-Japan film and television co-productions, launched on the Tokyo International Film Festival market TIFFCOM’s opening day at the “Taiwan Originals: Project Showcase” event.

	The fund aims to raise NT$100 million (about $3.1 million) and invest in at least five projects across film, television and animation over its first two years. Fundraising has reached 70% of the target, and the fund expects to begin operations by year-end, founder Chang Chen-yu told Variety.
	

	The name “Daily” reflects the idea that meaningful progress is built through daily efforts, Chang said at the launch.

	In Japan, Daily Capital has identified K2 Pictures and Remow as co-development partners. Founded by producer Kii Muneyuki, K2 Pictures brings together Japanese filmmakers including Iwai Shunji, Miike Takashi, Nishikawa Miwa and Kore-eda Hirokazu. Remow is backed by Japanese entertainment and media companies including Shueisha, Toei, Amuse, Shochiku, TBS Holdings and Fuji Media Holdings, with access to established IP libraries and distribution networks.

	“Investment amounts will vary according to each project’s scale and needs, whether it’s a film, series or animation. We expect to come in during development or pre-production, contribute to script discussions and help assemble the core creative team. We also aim to keep the primary capital recovery period within three years,” Chang said.

	The fund plans to pair Japan’s IP and production know-how with Taiwan’s flexible financing and co-production experience. It will also tap local production incentives and distribution networks to reach audiences beyond Japanese- and Mandarin-speaking markets.
	

	Its first announced investment is the series “Love Ends in Bloom.” Set in 1930s Chiayi and Alishan, the 10-episode historical romance and business drama follows a Japanese geisha who devises a cross-border marriage scheme to save her mother, then falls into a forbidden romance with a Taiwanese timber magnate. The story unfolds during the Japanese colonial period (1895–1945), when Taiwan’s cypress industry was thriving, and views the era through a Japanese woman’s eyes.

	The project grew out of Chang’s return to his hometown of Chiayi in 2023. The railway station was under renovation, prompting him to reflect on the city’s forestry and railway history. “Despite our proximity, Taiwan, Japan and Korea are rarely seen together in one narrative,” Chang said in a previous interview with Variety.

	Written by Juliana Hsu, whose credits include period drama “Gold Leaf,” and directed by Sun Jie-heng, director of wartime historical drama “Three Tears in Borneo,” “Love Ends in Bloom” is slated to begin filming in February 2027, targeting a mid-2028 release.

	“The fund will measure success by whether its projects reach Japanese broadcasters, regional platforms and global streamers, and meet projected returns,” Chang said. “Those results could help Daily Capital raise a larger second fund focused on Taiwan-Japan and wider Asian co-productions.”

schema.headline: Taiwan-Japan Film Fund Daily Capital Launches at Tokyo Market, Backs Period Romance ‘Love Ends in Bloom’
